question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

For a month-to-month tenancy, check whether the notice is a **“no specified reason” notice under section 263**. Such a notice must give a termination date at least **120 days after the notice was given**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A section 263 notice has **no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act**. Seeking repairs may involve exercising repair rights: for example, the Act provides procedures for requesting urgent repairs and for giving written notice of non-urgent repairs. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Receiving the notice on the same day as following up the repairs may therefore be relevant evidence, but the document does not say that timing alone proves retaliation.

Also check that the notice:

- is in the prescribed form;
- is addressed to you;
- is signed by the landlord or their agent; and
- states the termination date. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A section 263 notice does **not** have to state a reason. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- **Confirm that the notice relies on section 263.** The retaliation rule in section 266(2) expressly applies to notices under sections **261 and 263**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Keep evidence** showing when and how you requested or followed up the repairs and when the notice was given. The retrieved Act does not specify a particular evidentiary checklist.
- **Apply to VCAT to challenge the notice within 60 days after it was given.** After that 60-day period, the Act says you are not entitled to apply to challenge a section 263 notice’s validity. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- If the landlord later seeks a possession order, VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice and that the notice has not been withdrawn. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

If the notice relies on another ground—such as the landlord claiming that major repairs require vacant possession—the specific retaliation rule above may not apply. A repairs-based notice under section 255 instead requires necessary permits and consents, work that cannot properly be done while you remain, and at least **60 days’ notice**; it may be challenged at VCAT within **30 days** after it is given. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: All three points are covered. The answer says a section 263 'no specified reason' notice must give at least 120 days. It says the notice has 'no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act', with repair requests as the example. It also says the tenant can 'Apply to VCAT to challenge the notice within 60 days after it was given.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says the opposite of the first condition, stating 'A section 263 notice does **not** have to state a reason', and gives the challenge deadline as 'within 60 days after it was given'; the 30-day period applies only to a different, hypothetical section 255 notice ('If the notice relies on another ground...').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, dated 2 July 2019' (linked as 97-109aa088), which was in force on 1 November 2019, and every rule it applies (ss 255, 263, 266(2)) comes from that version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**, a rental provider must not unreasonably refuse permission to keep a pet. To refuse, they must apply to VCAT **within 14 days after receiving the official request**; otherwise, they are taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because you sent the form **three weeks ago**, the owner is taken to have consented **if the request was validly given to the rental provider and no VCAT application was made within those 14 days**. The agent simply saying “no” because the owner is allergic is not, by itself, the required VCAT application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If an application was lodged on time, VCAT decides whether refusal is reasonable. It may consider the type of pet, the nature of the apartment and its fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, and anything else it considers relevant. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved Act does not say whether an owner’s allergy—especially where the owner rarely visits—would be enough, so that outcome cannot be predicted from the document.

## What you can do

Ask the agent in writing:

1. whether the owner applied to VCAT within the **14-day period**; and  
2. for the application or case details if they say they did. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If no timely application was made, you can state that the owner is taken to have consented under **section 71C(2)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Keep the request form and evidence of when it was delivered.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the output says a rental provider must 'apply to VCAT within 14 days after receiving the official request; otherwise, they are taken to have consented'; it applies this to the facts, saying that because the form was sent 'three weeks ago, the owner is taken to have consented if the request was validly given to the rental provider and no VCAT application was made within those 14 days'; and it gives the next step 'Ask the agent in writing: whether the owner applied to VCAT within the 14-day period.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not say the refusal stands, does not put the burden on the renter, and does not treat the allergy as decisive. It says the agent's "no" "is not, by itself, the required VCAT application," states that the rental provider "must apply to VCAT within 14 days," and says whether the owner's allergy would be enough "cannot be predicted from the document."

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

**The notice does not automatically disappear because the buyer pulled out.** Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025**, a notice to vacate is withdrawn **only** by a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the landlord and the renter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

However, a sale notice is permitted only where the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**, and it must give at least **60 days’ notice** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the property is no longer being sold or offered for sale, you can challenge whether the notice remains valid; VCAT can determine its validity [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

You do **not** have to leave merely because the termination date arrives. To obtain a possession order, the landlord must apply to VCAT, and VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making the order is reasonable and proportionate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord to **withdraw the notice in writing**, with the withdrawal signed by both sides [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If they refuse, you may apply to **VCAT to challenge the notice’s validity**. For a sale notice, the Act says that application must be made within **30 days after the notice was given**, although a challenge may also be raised on or before the hearing of a possession-order application [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the landlord applies for possession, tell VCAT that the buyer withdrew and provide any evidence showing that the property is no longer being sold or offered for sale with vacant possession [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Bottom line:** the failed sale does not itself formally withdraw the notice, but it may undermine the basis for enforcing it. Do not treat the notice as withdrawn unless the required written withdrawal is signed [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No: the answer covers the 60-day minimum notice period, written withdrawal signed by both parties, and next steps (ask for a signed written withdrawal or challenge at VCAT within 30 days). It is missing the first point: it never says the outcome depends on the ground stated in the notice and the evidence attached to it, and never distinguishes a planned sale with vacant possession from a signed contract. It only says generally that a sale notice requires the premises to be 'sold or offered for sale with vacant possession'.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

You **do not have to pay the higher rent based only on the agent’s informal email or the unsuccessful negotiation**. The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days’ notice in the prescribed form**, and an increase that does not comply is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The prescribed notice is **Form 5, “Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises.”** It must state the current and new rent, the start date, and the method and calculation used to determine the increase [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It may be delivered by email **only if you consented to electronic delivery** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Therefore, unless the email actually included a properly completed Form 5, you continue paying your **current rent** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If a valid notice is later given, the higher rent is payable from the start date stated in that notice, which must allow **at least 60 days’ notice** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The documents do not allow an exact commencement date to be calculated until a valid notice is given.

A further restriction applies if you are in a fixed term: rent cannot increase before the term ends unless the agreement provides for an increase of a specified amount or according to a specified calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Rent also cannot generally be increased at intervals of less than **12 months** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide a properly completed **Form 5** and to confirm its proposed start date and calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can state that you will continue paying the current rent until a valid notice takes effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

After receiving a valid notice, you have **30 days** to apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for a free investigation if you consider the proposed rent excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Documents in force on 1 October 2025:**

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110**, 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 004**, 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is named as the prescribed notice; the answer says the rental provider must give "at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form"; on the hardest point it states "unless the email actually included a properly completed Form 5, you continue paying your current rent" and that "an increase that does not comply is invalid"; and it gives next steps, including asking the agent for Form 5, continuing to pay the current rent, and applying to Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failure conditions are asserted: the answer says 'You do not have to pay the higher rent based only on the agent's informal email', that the increase applies from 'the start date stated in that notice, which must allow at least 60 days' notice', and that the notice 'may be delivered by email only if you consented to electronic delivery' (the '30 days' figure refers to the window for seeking a review, not the notice period).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

You **cannot simply repair the damage without telling the owner or agent**. A renter who becomes aware of damage must notify the residential rental provider **in writing as soon as practicable**, stating that the damage occurred and describing it. Damage caused by the dog is not ordinary “fair wear and tear,” and renters must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Repairs—urgent or non-urgent—must be done by a **suitably qualified person** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the owner gives you a repair notice, they may require you to repair the damage at your expense within **14 days** and in a proper, tradesman-like manner. If that is not done, the owner may arrange the repair at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, including photographs and a description of the damaged skirting boards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask whether they will allow you to arrange the repair.
3. If they agree, use a **suitably qualified person**, keep the invoice and take before-and-after photographs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. Before leaving, ensure the premises are, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

The retrieved documents **do not say whether repairing the damage—or failing to disclose it before repair—would affect the owner’s property insurance**. That depends on the insurance policy, so I cannot answer that part from these documents.

**Law applied as at 15 October 2026:**

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, dated 13 October 2026, **Authorised Version No. 115** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, dated 30 June 2026, **Authorised Version No. 009** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

On the hardest point, it says 'Damage caused by the dog is not ordinary “fair wear and tear”' and that the owner can require repair 'at your expense', and it says the premises must be left 'in the same condition as when you moved in'. It states that the documents 'do not say whether repairing the damage... would affect the owner’s property insurance'. It also gives next steps, such as 'Notify the owner or agent in writing now'.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The applicable retrieved document is the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

- The document **does not prescribe a minimum number of power circuits** for a rental property. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The electrical minimum standard requiring every power outlet and lighting circuit to be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual current devices did **not begin until 29 March 2023**, so it was not yet operating on 1 March 2023. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- However, the rental provider had to arrange an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided **every 2 years**, conducted by a licensed or registered electrician. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Report the repeated tripping in writing** and ask the rental provider to have a suitably qualified electrician inspect and repair the circuit; the prescribed rental agreement says repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask for the date of the most recent electrical safety check.** You may also request a copy of the most recent check in writing; it must be supplied **within 7 days** and must include the results, repairs required and action taken. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. If treated as a **non-urgent repair**, the rental provider must complete it within a reasonable time, and you may apply to VCAT for a repair order if it remains undone **14 days after written notice**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
4. The retrieved document does not establish that tripping only when a kettle and portable heater run together is automatically an urgent repair. It says urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of an essential service or a rental-provider-supplied appliance for heating, cooking, hot water or laundering. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

So, you can ask for an **electrical inspection and whatever repair or circuit upgrade the electrician finds necessary**, but these documents do not give you a direct right to demand a particular number of circuits. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?

## What the law says

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document on **15 October 2026** is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- You must not assign or sublet any part of your rental without the rental provider’s **written consent**. An unauthorised assignment or subletting is invalid unless VCAT has determined that consent is unnecessary. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent could give **you** a notice to vacate for assigning, subletting or purportedly subletting without consent. That notice must provide a termination date at least **14 days** after it is given. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- Whether your friend is a **sub-renter** or merely someone staying with your permission depends on the arrangement. The retrieved documents do not contain enough information to classify it—particularly whether your friend pays rent or has exclusive possession of a room.

## What you can do

1. **Ask your friend to agree in writing to leave** on a specified date. A residential rental agreement can be terminated by agreement between the rental provider and renter. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. If they do not agree, the correct legal process depends on their status:
   - If they occupy the premises **solely**, are not a renter under a residential rental agreement, and remain after your permission has ended, a person claiming entitlement to possession may apply to VCAT under section 344. This procedure only applies where the premises are occupied **solely** by that person and were rented premises within the previous **12 months**. [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
   - If you still live there with your friend, that “sole occupation” procedure does not fit the wording of section 344. [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
   - The retrieved documents do **not** state what eviction procedure you personally can use against a friend who shares the home with you and is neither a valid sub-renter nor a sole occupant. I therefore cannot say from these documents that you can simply issue them a prescribed notice to vacate.

3. **Do not assume you can personally force them out.** Where VCAT makes a possession order and a warrant is required, the warrant is directed to a police officer or authorised person, who may compel occupants to leave. [[12]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because the documents do not resolve the shared-home situation without more facts, you should obtain advice about your friend’s legal status before changing locks or removing their belongings. Also be aware that telling the agent may expose the unauthorised subletting and allow the rental provider to issue **you** the 14-day notice described above. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

On the hardest point, the output says status 'depends on the arrangement' and names deciding facts: 'whether your friend pays rent or has exclusive possession of a room.' It also states that you must not assign or sublet 'without the rental provider's written consent.'

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the applicable document was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- The landlord had a duty to maintain the premises **in good repair**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- For a month-to-month tenancy, the landlord could issue a **“no specified reason” notice** under section 263, but the termination date had to be **at least 120 days after the notice was given**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A section 263 notice had **no effect** if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Asking the landlord to meet the statutory repair duty—and using the repair procedures in sections 72–75—may therefore be relevant to whether section 266(2) applies. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- You could not apply to VCAT to challenge a section 263 notice after **60 days from the date it was given**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What to check and do

1. **Check which section the notice uses.** If it is a section 263 “no specified reason” notice, check that it gives at least **120 days** and consider whether it followed your repair request in retaliation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Keep evidence of timing:** your repair requests and follow-ups, the landlord or agent’s replies, photographs of the leaks, and the notice received the same day. The retrieved Act does not state a specific evidentiary test for proving retaliation.
3. **Apply to VCAT within 60 days** to challenge a retaliatory section 263 notice. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
4. **Check the notice’s form:** it must use the prescribed form, be addressed to you, be signed by the landlord or agent, and specify the termination date; a section 263 notice does not have to state a reason. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
5. If the notice instead claims the premises must be vacated for **repairs**, section 255 required necessary permits and consents, required that the work could not properly be done while you remained, and required at least **60 days’ notice**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retaliation rule in section 266(2) expressly covers sections **261 and 263**, not section 255. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The output says a section 263 'no specified reason' notice needs 'at least 120 days after the notice was given', and that it 'had no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act'. Asking for repairs is hedged only as 'may therefore be relevant', but the rule itself is stated clearly. It also says to 'Apply to VCAT within 60 days to challenge a retaliatory section 263 notice'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer does not say the landlord needed to give a reason, and states that "a section 263 notice does not have to state a reason". The only VCAT challenge deadline it gives is 60 days ("Apply to VCAT within 60 days"); the 120-day and section 255 60-day figures are notice periods, not challenge deadlines.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019' (link 97-109aa088), the version in force on 1 November 2019. It applies ss 263 and 266(2)–(3) and every other rule it uses from that version only, without relying on any version that was not in force on that date.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says on 1 October 2025

The applicable law is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025**, and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

- A property must be advertised or offered at a **fixed rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or invite** an offer above the advertised rent. Breaching this rule is an offence carrying up to **60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 penalty units for a body corporate**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- A false or misleading representation about the rent in an advertisement is also prohibited and carries the same maximum penalties. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Merely hearing that another applicant made an **unsolicited** higher offer does not, by itself, establish that the agent invited rental bidding. The version in force on 1 October 2025 does not expressly prohibit accepting an unsolicited higher offer. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Relisting at a higher fixed rent is not expressly prohibited by these documents. It could support a complaint if the original price was misleading or the relisting was part of soliciting higher bids, but it does not prove a breach by itself. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The false statement that you withdrew is concerning, but the retrieved documents do not create a specific offence or remedy merely because an unsuccessful applicant was incorrectly recorded as having withdrawn. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Write immediately to the agent and rental provider** saying you did not withdraw. Ask them to correct their records and explain:
   - who marked the application withdrawn and when;
   - whether anyone invited applicants to offer above the advertised rent; and
   - whether the property was offered or allocated at a higher rent.  
   The retrieved documents do not say they must provide you with reasons or give you the property. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

2. **Report the suspected rental-bidding or misleading-advertising conduct to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria.** The Director’s functions include monitoring compliance with the Act. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

3. **A direct VCAT challenge is uncertain.** VCAT has jurisdiction over matters involving a proposed residential rental agreement and can restrain breaches or award compensation in matters properly before it, but the retrieved provisions do not clearly give an unsuccessful applicant a direct right to obtain the property or compensation for a breach of sections 30F or 30G. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## Evidence to save

The documents do not provide a specific evidence checklist. To preserve evidence relevant to the statutory issues, save:

- the original advertisement showing the property, fixed rent, URL, and date/time;
- your completed application and submission confirmation showing the rent you applied at;
- the full “you withdrew” email, including headers and attachments;
- your written response stating that you did not withdraw;
- screenshots of the new advertisement showing the higher rent and date/time;
- every email, text, platform message, or call note suggesting that you increase your offer or compete with another applicant;
- any firsthand message or statement from the person who says a higher offer was made, including exactly what they observed and when.

These records would help distinguish an unsolicited higher offer from prohibited conduct by the provider or agent **soliciting or inviting** one, and could help show whether the original rent advertisement was false or misleading. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered, and the hardest one is met by the statement that 'The version in force on 1 October 2025 does not expressly prohibit accepting an unsolicited higher offer.' The answer also says relisting at a higher fixed rent 'does not prove a breach by itself', that soliciting or inviting offers above the advertised rent is an offence, and that the documents 'do not create a specific offence or remedy' for the false withdrawal record.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three prohibited claims is made: the answer says relisting "does not prove a breach by itself," that the law "does not expressly prohibit accepting an unsolicited higher offer," and that the documents "do not say they must provide you with reasons or give you the property."

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, a rental provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to keep a pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

More importantly, if the owner did **not apply to VCAT within 14 days** after receiving your official request, the owner is legally taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Simply telling you “no” because the owner is allergic is not enough; they must have applied to VCAT within that period. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If they applied in time, VCAT decides whether refusal is reasonable. It may consider the type of pet, the apartment and its fixtures, any applicable legislation, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not say whether an owner’s allergy—particularly where the owner rarely visits—is by itself sufficient, so that cannot be determined from the retrieved document.

## What you can do

Ask the agent to confirm **whether and when the owner applied to VCAT**, and request the application details. If no application was made within 14 days, tell the agent that consent is taken to have been given under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If an application was made on time, you can explain to VCAT that the owner rarely visits and argue that the allergy does not make refusal reasonable. VCAT can either permit the dog or find that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

(1) The answer says the owner is taken to have consented if they did 'not apply to VCAT within 14 days after receiving your official request'. (2) It applies this to the user's situation: a 'no' is 'not enough; they must have applied to VCAT within that period', and 'If no application was made within 14 days, tell the agent that consent is taken to have been given'. (3) It gives a next step: 'Ask the agent to confirm whether and when the owner applied to VCAT'.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

**The notice does not automatically disappear because the buyer pulled out.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only through a written withdrawal signed by both the landlord and the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If the landlord still intends to **sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**, the sale ground may still apply even without that particular buyer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the property is no longer going to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession, you may challenge whether the notice remains valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

- Ask the landlord to formally withdraw the notice. The withdrawal must be **in writing and signed by both you and the landlord** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the notice was given within the last **30 days**, you may apply to VCAT to challenge its validity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the landlord seeks a possession order, VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making the possession order is **reasonable and proportionate** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

So, **you do not necessarily have to leave merely because the notice remains on foot**, but you should not assume the failed sale cancelled it. Seek a signed withdrawal or challenge the notice where appropriate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Applicable document:** *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (6 August 2025), **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110**, which was in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

**No—not on the facts given.** An ordinary email saying the rent will increase is not enough unless it gives you the prescribed **Form 5, “Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises.”** The form may be delivered by email only if you consented to electronic delivery. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A valid notice must:

- be in Form 5;
- give at least **60 days’ notice**;
- state the current and new rent, the start date, and the method and calculation used; and
- cover only one increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is **invalid**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Your unsuccessful negotiation does not replace the required notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You therefore continue paying your **current rent**. If a valid Form 5 is later given, the higher rent is payable from the start date specified in that form, which must be at least 60 days after the notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The rent generally cannot be increased more than once every **12 months**, or during a fixed term unless the agreement permits an increase of a specified amount or by a specified calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide the prescribed **Form 5** and tell them that you have not received a valid rent-increase notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) If you later receive one and consider the increase excessive, you can ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate by applying in writing within **30 days after the notice is given**. question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

The versions in force on **1 October 2025** were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version No. 110, 6 August 2025** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version No. 004, 1 July 2025** [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**Advertising:** These documents do not prohibit advertising a property merely because a photograph appears to show mould. However, before entering the rental agreement, the rental provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and whether, within the previous 3 years, they received a repair notice about structurally caused mould or damp [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). They also must not use misleading or deceptive conduct, or make false or misleading representations about the property’s characteristics, to induce someone to rent it [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The property must comply with the minimum standards **on or before the day the renter enters occupation** [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The mould standard requires **each room** to be free from mould and damp **caused by or related to the building structure** [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photograph enough proof?** Not necessarily. It may be useful evidence of the room’s condition, but the photograph alone may not establish that the marks are mould or that the mould is caused by or related to the building structure—the particular requirement in the minimum standard [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The prescribed condition-report guidance says photographs may be useful in a dispute, not that they are conclusive proof [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or rental provider, in writing:

1. whether the property currently complies with the rental minimum standards;  
2. whether the marks shown are mould or damp and whether they are structurally caused; and  
3. whether any mould or damp repair notice was received in the last 3 years [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

If you rent the property and it does not comply on or immediately after occupation, you may request **urgent repairs** to bring it up to the minimum standards [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Keep the advertisement and photographs; if you move in, record the issue in the condition report and add dated, labelled photographs identifying the room [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the mould standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'), the photo point ('the photograph alone may not establish that the marks are mould or that the mould is caused by or related to the building structure'), and next steps (ask the agent in writing, request urgent repairs).

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither forbidden thing, stating that the documents "do not prohibit advertising a property merely because a photograph appears to show mould" and that "the photograph alone may not establish that the marks are mould or that the mould is caused by or related to the building structure."

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

For a month-to-month tenancy, check whether the notice is a **section 263 “notice to vacate for no specified reason.”** Such a notice had to give a termination date **at least 120 days after it was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

A section 263 notice has **no effect** if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That is the relevant retaliation protection. The document does not establish from timing alone that the notice was retaliatory.

## What you can do or ask

- Check that the notice relies on **section 263**. The retaliation rule in section 266(2) expressly applies only to notices under **section 261 or section 263** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Check whether the termination date is at least **120 days after 1 November 2019** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Keep your repair requests, follow-up messages, and the notice showing they occurred on the same day; the retrieved document does not specify what evidence is required, but these materials concern whether the notice was given in response to your request.
- You may apply to the Tribunal to challenge a section 263 notice, but must do so **within 60 days after the notice was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the notice instead claims the property must be vacated for repairs under **section 255**, check whether the landlord intends to do the work immediately after the termination date, has all necessary permits and consents, and whether the work cannot properly be done while you remain. That notice must provide at least **60 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Section 266(2)’s retaliation rule does not expressly cover a section 255 notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The hardest point is covered by 'You may apply to the Tribunal to challenge a section 263 notice, but must do so within 60 days after the notice was given', where the Tribunal is VCAT.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?

## What the law says

However, a sale notice is permitted only if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**. If the landlord is no longer selling or offering the property for sale, you can challenge whether the notice remains valid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You cannot be forcibly removed merely because the notice date arrives. The landlord must obtain a VCAT possession order. VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making a possession order is reasonable and proportionate. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- If the landlord applies for possession, attend the hearing and explain that the buyer withdrew and, if applicable, that the property is no longer being sold. VCAT—not the landlord alone—decides whether you must leave. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

**So:** unless formally withdrawn, the notice remains on foot, but whether you ultimately have to leave depends on whether the property is still genuinely being sold or offered for sale and whether VCAT makes a possession order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

You **do not have to pay the higher rent** unless the rental provider gives you a valid notice in the prescribed form. An ordinary email saying the rent will increase—and later negotiations—does not replace that notice. A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid. This is under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110**, in force on 1 October 2025. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed notice is **Form 5, “Notice of proposed rent increase to renter of rented premises”**, under the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004**. It must state the current and new rent, start date, and the method and calculation used to determine the increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A valid Form 5 notice may be delivered by email **if you consented to email delivery**, but it must provide at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Therefore, you continue paying your current rent until the start date in a valid notice—which must be at least 60 days after that notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The rent also cannot generally be increased more than once every **12 months**, or during a fixed term unless the agreement permits an increase of a specified amount or by a specified calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent to provide the required **Form 5 notice** and calculate the start date using at least 60 days’ notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Continue paying the existing rent until a valid increase takes effect. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If you receive Form 5 and believe the amount is excessive, you may ask Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate by applying in writing within **30 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. Form 5 is named as the prescribed notice, and the answer requires at least 60 days' notice. It says the email does not replace the notice, so the higher rent is not payable yet: 'An ordinary email saying the rent will increase—and later negotiations—does not replace that notice. A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid.' It also gives next steps, including continuing to pay the existing rent and asking Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate.

The answer says none of the failing claims: it states "You do not have to pay the higher rent unless the rental provider gives you a valid notice in the prescribed form," ties the start date to a valid notice giving "at least 60 days' notice" rather than to the email, and says notice "may be delivered by email if you consented to email delivery."

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

You **cannot simply repair the damage without telling the owner**. You must notify the rental provider **in writing, as soon as practicable**, that the damage occurred and describe its nature. Email or another permitted electronic communication may be used. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Damage caused intentionally or negligently is not fair wear and tear. When moving out, you must leave the premises, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The owner may issue a repair notice requiring you to repair the damage at your expense within **14 days**. The work must be completed in a **proper and tradesman-like manner**; otherwise, the owner may arrange the repair at your expense. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The standard rental agreement also says that only a **suitably qualified person** may perform repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Notify the owner or agent in writing now, include photos, and ask whether they agree to you arranging a suitably qualified person to repair the skirting boards before you leave. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not expressly say that you may independently repair renter-caused damage before the owner responds.

## Insurance

The documents **do not say whether this damage or your proposed repair would affect the owner’s insurance coverage, premium or ability to claim**, so I cannot answer that from the retrieved material. They only say that a rental agreement cannot make you **liable by default for the excess** under the owner’s insurance policy. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

**Law applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**; and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 009**, dated **30 June 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) It requires written notice as soon as practicable: "You must notify the rental provider in writing, as soon as practicable." (2) It says intentional or negligent damage is not fair wear and tear, that the premises must be left in the same condition, and that the renter can be required to repair "at your expense". (3) It states that "the documents do not say whether this damage or your proposed repair would affect the owner's insurance." (4) It gives a next step: "Notify the owner or agent in writing now, include photos, and ask whether they agree to you arranging a suitably qualified person to repair."

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 March 2023**, the retrieved law does **not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental property. The electrical minimum standard requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual current devices does not start until **29 March 2023**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, the rental provider must maintain the premises **in good repair and fit for occupation**, and electrical repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

This comes from the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002**, dated **31 May 2022** and in force from **1 June 2022**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Notify the rental provider **in writing** that the breaker repeatedly trips when the kettle and heater operate together, and ask for a suitably qualified person to assess and repair the electrical installation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- Ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check. The provider must arrange a check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they supplied **every 2 years**, performed by a licensed or registered electrician, and provide the date on request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- If treated as a **non-urgent repair**, the provider must complete it within a reasonable time. If it remains undone **14 days after receiving your written notice**, you may apply to VCAT for a repair order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved document does not establish that this particular tripping problem is automatically an urgent repair, nor does it give you a specific entitlement to an additional circuit. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. The answer says the law 'does not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits', and it gives next steps: notify the provider in writing to arrange a qualified repair, and 'ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states the law 'does **not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits**', and says the circuit breaker/RCD standard 'does not start until **29 March 2023**', so it does not claim that standard already applies on 1 March 2023.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Yes—coin-operated washing machines are not expressly prohibited.** The law requires a rooming house to provide, in good working order, **one washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the house’s maximum capacity. It does not state that use must be free. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

If the operator charges for laundry services, they must give you:

- **before you move in**, a separate schedule showing the amount charged for those services; and  
- if you use them, an **itemised account showing your individual use**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

This comes from the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** (in force from 13 October 2026), sections 109 and 142B, [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version No. 2** (1 December 2024), regulation 14. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

**What you can do:** Ask the operator for the required schedule of laundry charges and an itemised account of your use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You can also ask whether two machines are enough: the requirement is one machine for every 12 or fewer residents, calculated using the rooming house’s **maximum capacity**, not just its current occupancy. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable documents were the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)**. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

- At that date, there was **no specific provision banning an advertisement merely because the premises might not meet the rental minimum standards**. The express advertising prohibition in section 65B was not yet in Authorised Version No. 110; it appears in the later Authorised Version No. 111, in force from **25 November 2025**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- However, a provider or agent must not use misleading or deceptive conduct to induce someone to enter an agreement, or make a false or misleading representation about the premises’ characteristics. [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The minimum standard requires **each room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure**. Mould from another cause is not expressly covered by that particular minimum standard. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- A photo that only *looks like* mould does **not necessarily prove non-compliance**: it may not establish that the substance is mould, that it still exists, or that it was caused by or related to the building structure. The retrieved documents do not state that a photograph alone is sufficient proof. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Before signing, ask the provider to disclose:

1. **whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards**; and  
2. whether, within the last **3 years**, the provider received a repair notice concerning mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

If you take the property and it does not comply on or immediately after you enter, you may request **urgent repairs** to bring it up to the minimum standards. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Keep a copy of the advertisement and photographs, but the retrieved documents do not say that those images alone conclusively prove a breach.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the mould and damp standard ('each room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'), the photo not proving a breach ('A photo that only looks like mould does not necessarily prove non-compliance... The retrieved documents do not state that a photograph alone is sufficient proof'), and next steps (ask the provider about compliance before signing, and request urgent repairs after moving in).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable law is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Merely saying that a friend “moved in” does not establish from these documents whether there was a **subletting arrangement**. If it was subletting, you needed the rental provider’s **written consent**. A subletting without that consent is invalid unless VCAT determined that consent was unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider could give **you** a notice to vacate for unauthorised subletting. The termination date must be at least **14 days after the notice is given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

- **Ask your friend to agree in writing to leave by a stated date.**
- **Do not personally use force to remove them.** The prescribed notice explains that forcible eviction may only be carried out by Victoria Police acting under a VCAT warrant for possession. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- If your friend refuses, the retrieved documents **do not clearly state what legal process a renter must use to remove an unauthorised occupant who may not be a valid sub-renter**. I cannot tell from these documents whether you should use a notice to vacate, another VCAT procedure, or a different legal process.
- You should therefore obtain tenancy-law advice before changing locks or removing their belongings. Also be aware that notifying the agent may expose you to the **14-day notice-to-vacate risk** described above. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed forms are in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009**, incorporating amendments in force from 30 June 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
